extracted.intended_audience: contributors to mathlib (Lean 4) / developers writing Lean 4 code and theorems for Mathlib
extracted.subtask_description: A style guide for naming files, declarations, theorems, symbols, and other identifiers in mathlib under Lean 4. It specifies capitalization, spelling, symbol-to-word mappings, and many idiomatic naming patterns to make names discoverable and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: File name case
rubrics_metrics.description: Files in mathlib should generally be named in UpperCamelCase (with .lean extension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very rare exception are files named after some specifically lower-cased object (e.g. lp.lean for a file specifically about the space ℓ_p). Such exceptions should be discussed on Zulip first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall capitalization scheme (Prop / Type / other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of snake_case, lowerCamelCase and UpperCamelCase according to the following: Terms of Props (e.g. proofs, theorem names) use snake_case; Props and Types (or Sorts) (inductive types, structures, classes) are in UpperCamelCase; all other terms of Types are in lowerCamelCase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions are named the same way as their return values (e.g. a function of type A → B → C is named as though it is a term of type C). When something named with UpperCamelCase is part of something named with snake_case, it is referenced in lowerCamelCase. Rules 1-6 apply to fields of a structure or constructors of an inductive type in the same way. There are rare exceptions (e.g., Ne rather than NE, outParam) — any such exceptions should be discussed on Zulip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function naming follows return type
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions are named the same way as their return values (e.g. a function of type A → B → C is named as though it is a term of type C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the capitalization scheme: it ensures functions that return a Type/Prop follow the naming case for that return value. See examples such as Continuous.fun_mul vs Continuous.mul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronym casing
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms like LE are written upper-/lowercase as a group, depending on what the first character would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same grouping rule when deciding whether an acronym segment is UpperCamelCase, lowerCamelCase, or snake_case. Exceptions to preserve local naming symmetry are acceptable but should be discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and local symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Some names are exceptions to the general rules to preserve local naming symmetry (examples: Ne rather than NE; outParam despite Sort output; interval names like Set.Icc where the I is capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exceptions are rare and should be discussed on Zulip. Older files may not follow conventions; PRs to rename are welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Declaration names use American English spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: factorization, Localization, FiberBundle (not factorisation, Localisation, FibreBundle). Contrast this with documentation, which may use other common English spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol-to-word naming dictionary
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating symbols into words, use the provided shortcuts and names (e.g., ∨ → or, ∧ → and, → → r/of/imp, ↔ → iff, ¬ → not, ∃ → ex/bex, ∀ → fo/forall/ball, = → eq, ≠ → ne, ∘ → comp, set symbols like ∈ → mem, ∪ → union, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed shortcuts for logic, set, algebra, and lattice symbols. Note: ball and bex are used for bounded quantifiers in Lean core but should not be used in mathlib. For set shortcuts, use sUnion, iUnion, biUnion with the indicated conventions (i for indexed, bi for bounded indexed, s for 'set').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering relation naming (≤ and <)
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathlib, prefer using ≤ and < (le/lt) in names instead of ≥ and >, so both le/lt and ge/gt are available for naming ≤ and <.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ge/gt when arguments appear in different orders, to match argument order of another relation, to describe the relation with arguments swapped, or if the second argument is 'more variable'. Use le/lt for the first occurrence of ≤/< in the theorem name; ge/gt indicates swapped arguments. Examples and rationale are provided in multiple theorem name examples (lt_iff_le_not_ge, not_le_of_gt, ge_trans, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot notation and namespace usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Dots are used for namespaces and automatically generated names (recursors, eliminators, structure projections), and may be introduced manually where projector notation is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include And.intro, And.elim, Prod.fst, LE.trans, LT.trans_le, etc. Note that types in UpperCamelCase get lowerCamelCased when they appear in theorem names, so namespace patterns like And.* remain coherent with the symbol dictionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic description names
rubrics_metrics.description: Common axiomatic properties and operations use short canonical names for unfolding/properties (e.g., def for unfolding a definition; refl, irrefl, symm, trans, antisymm, asymm, congr, comm, assoc, left_comm, right_comm, mul_left_cancel, mul_right_cancel, inj).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These names should be used when describing theorems axiomatically rather than stating full conclusions. This provides uniform, discoverable names for common algebraic/logical properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conventional single-letter names for certain categories: u,v,w,... for universes; α,β,γ,... for generic types; a,b,c,... for propositions; x,y,z,... for elements; h,h1,... for assumptions; p,q,r,... for predicates/relations; s,t,... for lists and sets; m,n,k,... for naturals; i,j,k,... for integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types with mathematical content are expressed with the usual uppercase letters (G for group, R for ring, K or 𝕜 for field, E for vector space). Older files may use Greek letters for all types — PRs to rename are welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Namespacing theorem names by operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Put common 'axiomatic' properties of an operation in a namespace that begins with the name of the operation (e.g., And.comm, Or.comm, And.intro, Or.intro_left).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps users guess theorem names and find them via tab completion. However, do not do this for axiomatic logical and arithmetic operations (e.g., and_assoc or mul_comm remain as standalone names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive theorem naming and short forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer descriptive names that state the conclusion; if a short prefix suffices, make the name even shorter (e.g., neg_neg, Nat.pred_succ, succ_ne_zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an operation is infix, theorem names follow suit (e.g., neg_mul_neg to describe -a * -b). If only a prefix of the description is enough, shorten accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using 'of' to separate hypotheses in theorem names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the word 'of' to separate hypotheses in a theorem name; list the hypotheses in the order they appear in the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a theorem with type A → B → C should be named C_of_A_of_B. This maintains natural reading order rather than reversing hypothesis order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicate prefix vs suffix (is/predicate placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most predicates should be added as prefixes (e.g., IsClosed (Icc a b) becomes isClosed_Icc, not Icc_isClosed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are widely used exceptions analogous to atoms already suffixed by the naming convention (e.g., use _inj for f a = f b ↔ a = b and therefore _injective for Injective f, _mono/_antitone/_strictMono, etc.). Predicates used as suffixes can be preceded by _left or _right to indicate left- or right-monotonicity (e.g., mul_left_monotone : Monotone (· * a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming Prop-valued classes (Is prefix)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Prop-valued classes: if the class is a noun then its name should begin with Is; if it is an adjective it need not begin with Is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: IsNormal is acceptable for 'normal subgroup', although Normal is also fine. IsTopologicalRing is preferred for 'topological ring' as we don't informally say 'the ring R is topological'. This differentiates noun-like assumptions from adjective-like ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of structural lemmas: ext / ext_iff and @[ext]
rubrics_metrics.description: A lemma of the form (∀ x, f x = g x) → f = g should be named .ext and labelled with the @[ext] attribute. A lemma of the form f = g ↔ ∀ x, f x = g x should be named .ext_iff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the @[ext] attribute on a structure auto-generates such lemmas. Auto-generated lemmas are written in terms of projections; sometimes a better statement (e.g., using coercions) should be written by hand and marked with @[ext].

rubrics_metrics.name: Injectivity lemma naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, injectivity lemmas should be written in terms of Function.Injective f using the full word 'injective' (typically named f_injective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form injective_f still appears; bidirectional equalities f x = f y ↔ x = y should be named f_inj. The .inj suffix is acceptable in appropriate namespaces. When an automatically generated .inj exists, and a bidirectional lemma is needed, name it .inj_iff. Left/right qualifiers in injectivity names should refer to the argument that changes (e.g., sub_right_inj for a - b = a - c ↔ b = c). Bidirectional injectivity lemmas are good candidates for @[simp].

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction vs recursion naming (induction/rec patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction/recursion principles should accept a motive argument. If the motive eliminates into Prop the name should contain 'induction'; if it eliminates into Sort u or Type u the name should contain 'rec'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, include 'on' when the value comes before constructions. Use T.induction_on / T.recOn when 'value first', and T.induction / T.rec when 'constructions first'. Variations are acceptable when necessary for disambiguation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpanded vs expanded function forms and fun_ prefix
rubrics_metrics.description: Because expressions like f * g and fun x ↦ f x * g x are definitionally equal but syntactically different, provide lemma variants for both forms when needed. Use mul for the unexpanded form and fun_mul for the expanded form (use fun_ prefix for other operations similarly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no disambiguation is needed because a lemma uses only the expanded form, the fun_ prefix is not required. Examples: Continuous.fun_mul vs Continuous.mul. Both deserve tagging with the fun_prop attribute. Apply the same convention for addition, subtraction, negation, powers and composition of functions.
